assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turned precision spectroscopy into a platform for exceptionally accurate timekeeping and tests of fundamental physics, with broad influence across atomic physics and metrology.
assessment.attribution: Katori and Ye made distinct, complementary contributions to the optical lattice clock and its experimental realization.
assessment.maturity: The method has been repeatedly demonstrated and refined over decades; its scientific impact and practical prospects are clear.
uncertainties: The balance between foundational invention and the wider community's role in advancing clock performance deserves careful review.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The trapped-ion program established a powerful route to quantum logic and computation, connecting influential theoretical proposals to precise control of individual atoms.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller provided central theoretical foundations, while Blatt led landmark experimental demonstrations; the three contributions are complementary.
assessment.maturity: The field has developed through sustained experimental progress, with trapped ions among the most mature quantum-computing platforms.
uncertainties: The achievement spans theory, demonstration and later engineering advances, so the prize's precise scope would need definition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter interfaces and atomic quantum memories made it possible to store and retrieve quantum states of light, an important step toward quantum networks and scalable quantum communication.
assessment.attribution: Polzik, Kimble and Lukin represent influential, complementary approaches to interfaces and memories; the broader field also includes substantial contributions from other groups.
assessment.maturity: The core effects and memory protocols are well established, while long-distance, high-efficiency network integration remains an active challenge.
uncertainties: The breadth of the field makes it difficult to draw a narrow boundary around the prizeworthy discovery and its principal contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg arrays and optical-lattice experiments opened new ways to simulate and control many-body quantum systems, with results that connect quantum optics to condensed matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Browaeys, Bloch and Lukin have made leading contributions across complementary experimental approaches to quantum simulation.
assessment.maturity: The platforms have produced reproducible, expanding bodies of work, though their reach as general-purpose simulators is still developing.
uncertainties: The rapid pace of progress makes it early to judge which results will prove most transformative.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light provides a concrete way to reduce measurement noise below the standard quantum limit and has become important in precision interferometry, including gravitational-wave detection.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied foundational theory, Kimble helped establish key experimental methods, and Schnabel advanced the technology toward high-performance interferometers.
assessment.maturity: The technique has been demonstrated in increasingly capable instruments and has delivered measurable gains in gravitational-wave observatories.
uncertainties: The work spans several generations of theory and experiment, and the selection of a small set of laureates would require a careful account of later contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Photonic crystals and band gaps gave physicists a powerful way to control light propagation, reshaping photonics and enabling a wide range of later devices and experiments.
assessment.attribution: Yablonovitch and John independently articulated central ideas, and Joannopoulos helped develop the theoretical and computational foundations that made the field accessible.
assessment.maturity: The concepts are well established and have had lasting influence, although applications vary in their reach and maturity.
uncertainties: The discovery has several independent origins and the credited list includes important contributions to distinct strands, making the award's scope consequential.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave atom interferometry created a sensitive measurement method for gravity, acceleration and rotations, extending precision measurement with atomic coherence.
assessment.attribution: Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich made distinct foundational contributions to atom interferometry and its precision-measurement applications.
assessment.maturity: The method has been demonstrated across laboratory and field settings, with substantial continuing work on robustness and practical deployment.
uncertainties: The field's impact is distributed across multiple interferometer types and later experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson was a landmark confirmation of a central part of particle physics and depended on detectors capable of finding a rare signal amid enormous backgrounds.
assessment.attribution: Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee represent leadership and detector-building contributions to ATLAS and CMS, but the discovery was the work of two very large collaborations.
assessment.maturity: The signal has been confirmed and characterized through extensive follow-up measurements over many years.
uncertainties: Attributing a collaboration-scale discovery to a handful of individuals is inherently difficult and risks obscuring the work of thousands of contributors.
